thesis: Read-your-writes is a per-session guarantee, so solve it per session: either route a user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write, or carry a replication position with the session and only read from replicas that have caught up to it.
pitch: With replicas, a user can write, refresh, and not see their own change, which feels like data loss. I wouldn't make all reads go to the primary; the guarantee only matters for the writer. The simple option is sticky-to-primary: after a write, mark the session and route that user's reads to the primary for a window a bit longer than typical replication lag. The precise option is a position token: the write returns the primary's log position, the client or session carries it, and a read is served only by a replica at or past that position, otherwise it waits briefly or falls back to the primary. For a single page you can also just render the value you wrote. I'd pick sticky-to-primary first and move to tokens if primary read load becomes a problem.

points.d: Only the session that wrote needs to see the write immediately. Other users can tolerate lag. Making all reads strongly consistent wastes the replicas.

points.h: Option 1: sticky reads to the primary
points.d: After a write, set a session flag or cookie with an expiry (for example 5–10 seconds, above p99 replication lag) and route that session's reads to the primary. Simple and robust; costs extra primary reads proportional to write rate.

The write returns a log position (an LSN, GTID or commit timestamp). Reads carry it; the router picks a replica whose applied position is at least that, or waits up to a small timeout, then falls back to the primary.
The client renders the value it just wrote instead of re-reading it. Works for simple forms; breaks when the server computes derived fields or other devices are involved.

points.h: Monitor replication lag as a first-class metric
points.d: Every option depends on lag staying bounded. Alert on p99 lag, and have the router stop using replicas that fall too far behind.
If the user writes on a phone and reads on a laptop, a cookie on one device doesn't help. Store the last-write position against the user id instead.

decision: Sticky-to-primary when write volume is modest and primary has headroom. Position tokens when primary read capacity is the bottleneck or lag varies widely. Client echo for single-screen flows. Always pair with lag monitoring and replica eviction.
numbers: Sticky window sizing: set it above p99 replication lag. If p99 lag is 800 ms, a 5 second window is generous and costs one primary read per page view for 5 seconds after each write.
Extra primary load ≈ writes/sec × reads per session in the window. 200 writes/sec × 10 reads in the window = 2,000 extra primary reads/sec.
pitfalls: Fixed sticky window shorter than lag spikes: the bug reappears during peak, exactly when it's hardest to debug.
Ignoring cross-device and cross-service reads: a write through service A and a read through service B with its own replica.
Caches in front of replicas: the replica caught up but the cache still holds the old value.
Routing all reads to the primary after an incident 'temporarily' and never undoing it.

followups.q: What about monotonic reads, so a user never sees time go backwards?
followups.a: Pin a session to one replica, or carry the highest position seen and never read from a replica behind it. Position tokens give you both guarantees with one mechanism.

followups.q: A replica falls 30 seconds behind. What happens?
followups.a: With tokens, reads for recent writers fall back to the primary automatically. The router should also eject the replica from rotation past a lag threshold.

followups.q: How do you do this with a cache in front?
followups.a: Invalidate or update the cache on write in the same request path, or version cache entries with the position so a stale entry is detectable.

example: A user updates their shipping address and is redirected to the profile page. The write sets a 'recent-write' marker valid for 5 seconds, so the profile read goes to the primary and shows the new address. After 5 seconds the user's reads return to replicas.

sources.title: Martin Kleppmann: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, chapter 5 (Replication)
